title: Why Does the Almighty Not Set Times for Judgment?
summary: Job widens his complaint from his own suffering to the suffering of the world. He describes land grabbers and creditors who strip the poor, the destitute who forage like wild donkeys and harvest food they cannot eat, and the murderers, adulterers, and thieves who work under cover of darkness. God, it seems, charges no one with wrong. The chapter then describes the brief life and sudden end of the wicked, and Job dares anyone to prove him a liar.
story: This chapter continues Job's reply to Eliphaz's third speech (chapter 22). In chapter 23 Job spoke of his personal longing to find God. Here he steps back and looks at the whole social order, and he sees the same absence of justice everywhere. Eliphaz had accused Job of oppressing widows and orphans (22:6-9). Job answers, in effect, that such oppression is real and widespread, but the oppressors are not being punished, which is the opposite of what Eliphaz's theology requires. In the next chapter Bildad will reply with only a few lines, and the dialogue with the friends will begin to break down. The chapter's closing section (verses 18-24), which seems to describe the downfall of the wicked, is one of the most debated passages in the book.
historical:
The chapter pictures the agrarian society of the ancient Near East, where most people farmed small plots, the powerful controlled land and credit, and a bad harvest or a debt could push a family into destitution. Moving boundary stones (verse 2) was a way of seizing a neighbor's land by quietly shifting the markers that defined fields. Israel's law and wisdom literature condemn it more than once (Deuteronomy 19:14, 27:17; Proverbs 22:28), and boundary stones in Mesopotamia sometimes carried curses on anyone who moved them.

The practices Job describes, taking a widow's ox in pledge (verse 3), seizing a nursing child for a debt (verse 9), and driving the poor into the wilderness, reflect a world where debt could lead to the loss of livestock, land, and even family members sold or pledged into servitude. Israel's law sought to limit these practices (Exodus 22:25-27; Deuteronomy 24:6, 10-13, 17), and the prophets denounced them. Job's point is that they happen openly and without visible consequence.
cultural:
Verses 5-11 describe the life of the landless poor with painful precision. They forage in the wasteland like wild donkeys, gleaning in the vineyards of the wicked (verse 6); gleaning, gathering what the harvesters leave behind, was the right of the poor in Israel (Deuteronomy 24:19-21), but here it is the only way to survive. They sleep exposed to cold and mountain rain, huddling against rocks for shelter. Most bitter of all, they work as laborers for others: they carry sheaves but go hungry, crush olives and tread grapes in the winepresses but go thirsty (verses 10-11). Olive presses and wine vats cut into rock or built within walled enclosures were common across the region.

The second half of the description turns to crimes of the night (verses 13-17). Houses in the region were usually built of mud brick, and a thief could dig through a wall rather than break down a door (verse 16; compare Exodus 22:2 and Matthew 6:19). The murderer, the adulterer, and the burglar all prefer darkness, and Job calls them rebels against the light. For them deep darkness is their morning.
literary: The chapter is a lament about the world's injustice, built from a series of portraits. It opens with a question that frames everything (verse 1), then moves through three scenes: the oppressors and their victims in the countryside (verses 2-12), the criminals of the night in the city (verses 13-17), and the fate of the wicked (verses 18-24). Verse 12 is the hinge of the first half, joining the groaning of the city to the charge that God charges no one with wrongdoing. The final section is difficult because it seems to say what the friends have said, that the wicked vanish like foam and are carried off by Sheol. Some interpreters think the passage belongs to one of the friends, perhaps to Zophar, who has no third speech. Others read it as Job quoting the friends' view in order to reject it, or as a curse Job wishes on the wicked (several translations render the verbs as may they be), or as Job's own admission that the wicked do eventually die, though not in the way the friends claim. The chapter ends with Job's challenge in verse 25.

outline.t: Why does God not set times for judgment?
The oppressed poor and their oppressors
Rebels against the light: the murderer, adulterer, and thief
The brief life and sudden end of the wicked
Who can prove me a liar?

doctrines.note: Job asks why God does not set times for judgment that the faithful can see (verse 1). The question assumes that God is the judge of the earth, which is why his apparent silence is so troubling. Scripture later speaks of an appointed day of judgment, but Job lives before that hope is clear.

The crimes Job lists are the same ones Israel's law forbids: moving boundary stones, exploiting widows and orphans, taking pledges that leave the poor without food or clothing, murder, adultery, and theft. The chapter shows the kind of society the law was given to prevent.

The chapter shows sin in both its social and personal forms: structures of debt and land control that crush the poor, and individual crimes of violence and lust hidden by darkness. Job treats both as rebellion against God's light.

words.note: Ani, poor or afflicted. It describes someone who is oppressed, humbled, or without resources, often with the sense of being at the mercy of others. It appears twice in the chapter, in verses 9 and 14. In the Psalms and the Prophets, God is repeatedly described as the defender of the ani.

Gazal, to seize, rob, or plunder. It appears three times in this chapter, beginning with the stolen flocks of verse 2, and it names the violent taking of what belongs to others. The same verb appears in the law's command not to rob one's neighbor (Leviticus 19:13).

Marad, to rebel. It is often used of political revolt against a king. In verse 13 Job describes the wicked as those who rebel against the light, treating their crimes as a revolt against the moral order God has set in the world.

Tiphlah, something unseemly, folly, or wrong. In verse 12 it stands behind the BSB's God charges no one with wrongdoing. The same word appears in 1:22, where the narrator says that Job did not charge God with wrongdoing. The echo is pointed: Job now accuses God of failing to charge the wicked.

christ: The chapter's picture of the poor, the widow, the orphan, and the hungry laborer is the same world into which Jesus came. He announced his mission in the synagogue at Nazareth as good news to the poor and freedom for the oppressed (Luke 4:18-19, drawing on Isaiah 61), and his teaching repeatedly took the side of those Job describes. The New Testament also answers Job's opening question: God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness through the man he has appointed, and he has given proof of this by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31). The link to Job is thematic. Job wanted to see God's days of judgment. The gospel announces that the judge has already come once, in humility, and will come again.

hard.q: Verses 18-24 seem to say the opposite of what Job has been arguing. Who is speaking?
hard.a: The difficulty is real, and there is no consensus. In chapter 21 Job denied that the wicked are quickly punished, yet these verses describe the wicked as foam on the water, forgotten by the womb, and cut off like heads of grain. One view is that the text has been disturbed and that these verses belong to one of the friends, since the third cycle is unusually short (Bildad speaks only six verses in chapter 25, and Zophar does not speak at all). A second view keeps the verses with Job but reads them as a quotation of the friends' position, which he then challenges in verse 25. A third reads the verbs as wishes or curses: may their portion be cursed, may Sheol take them. A fourth takes them as Job's own view that the wicked do eventually die, but only as everyone dies, so that their end is no proof of divine justice. Each reading has defenders. What is clear is that the chapter as a whole presses a question the friends cannot answer: why the Almighty does not set visible times for judgment.

questions: Job describes workers who harvest food they cannot eat. Where do you see similar injustice today, and how should people of faith respond?
Job says that God charges no one with wrongdoing (verse 12). Is it faithful or faithless to say something like that to God?
The criminals in verses 13-17 love darkness because it hides what they do. What in your own life do you prefer to keep in the dark?
